section.paragraph: How fast will the population age 55 years and older be increasing at the beginning of 2015? To answer this question, we have to evaluate $$f^{\prime}(15)$$ , where $$f^{\prime}$$ is the derivative of $$f$$ . But the rules of differentiation that we have developed up to now will not help us find the derivative of $$f$$ .

In this section, we will introduce another rule of differentiation called the Chain Rule. When used in conjunction with the rules of differentiation developed in the last two sections, the Chain Rule enables us to greatly enlarge the class of functions that we are able to differentiate. (In Exercise 72, we will use the Chain Rule to answer the question posed in the introductory example.)
section.heading: The Chain Rule
section.paragraph: Consider the function $$h(x) = \left( x^{2} + x + 1 \right)^{2}$$ . If we were to compute $$h^{\prime}(x)$$ using only the rules of differentiation from the previous sections, then our approach might be to expand $$h(x)$$ . Thus,
from which we find

But what about the function $$H(x) = \left( x^{2} + x + 1 \right)^{100}$$ ? The same technique may be used to find the derivative of the function $$H$$ , but the amount of work involved in this case would be prodigious! Consider, also, the function $$G(x) = \sqrt{x^{2} + 1}$$ . For each of the two functions $$H$$ and $$G$$ , the rules of differentiation of the previous sections cannot be applied directly to compute the derivatives $$H^{\prime}$$ and $$G^{\prime}$$ .

Observe that both $$H$$ and $$G$$ are composite functions; that is, each is composed of, or built up from, simpler functions. For example, the function $$H$$ is composed of the two simpler functions $$f(x) = x^{2} + x + 1$$ and $$g(x) = x^{100}$$ as follows:
$$\begin{array}{l} {H(x) = g\lbrack f(x)\rbrack = \left\lbrack f(x) \right\rbrack^{100}} \\ {\phantom{H(x)} = {(x^{2} + x + 1)}^{100}} \end{array}$$
In a similar manner, we see that the function $$G$$ is composed of the two simpler functions $$f(x) = x^{2} + 1$$ and $$g(x) = \sqrt{x}$$ . Thus,
$$\begin{array}{l} {G(x) = g\left\lbrack {f(x)} \right\rbrack = \sqrt{f(x)}} \\ {\phantom{G(x)} = \sqrt{x^{2} + 1}} \end{array}$$
As a first step toward finding the derivative $$h^{\prime}$$ of a composite function $$h = g \circ f$$ defined by $$h(x) = g\left\lbrack f(x) \right\rbrack$$ , we write

$$y = g\left\lbrack f(x) \right\rbrack = g(u)$$

The dependency of $$h$$ on $$g$$ and $$f$$ is illustrated in Figure 7. Since $$u$$ is a function of $$x$$ , we may compute the derivative of $$u$$ with respect to $$x$$ if $$f$$ is a differentiable function, obtaining $$du \slash dx = f^{\prime}(x)$$ . Next, if $$g$$ is a differentiable function of $$u$$ , we may compute the derivative of $$g$$ with respect to $$u$$ , obtaining $$dy \slash du = g^{\prime}(u)$$ . Now, since the function $$h$$ is composed of the function $$g$$ and the function $$f$$ , we might suspect that the rule $$h^{\prime}(x)$$ for the derivative $$h^{\prime}$$ of $$h$$ will be given by an expression that involves the rules for the derivatives of $$f$$ and $$g$$ . But how do we combine these derivatives to yield $$h^{\prime}$$ ?

section.paragraph: This question can be answered by interpreting the derivative of each function as the rate of change of that function. For example, suppose $$u = f(x)$$ changes three times as fast as $$x$$ —that is,
$$f^{\prime}(x) = \frac{\mathit{du}}{\mathit{dx}} = 3$$
And suppose $$y = g(u)$$ changes twice as fast as $$u$$ —that is,
$$g^{\prime}(u) = \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{du}} = 2$$
Then we would expect $$y = h(x)$$ to change six times as fast as $$x$$ —that is,
or, equivalently,
$$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{du}} \cdot \frac{\mathit{du}}{\mathit{dx}} = (2)(3) = 6$$
This observation suggests the following result, which we state without proof.

note.title: Rule 7: The Chain Rule
note.heading: Rule 7: The Chain Rule
note.paragraph: If $$h(x) = g\left\lbrack f(x) \right\rbrack$$ , then
$$h^{\prime}(x) = \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}g\lbrack f(x)\rbrack = g^{\prime}\lbrack f(x)\rbrack f^{\prime}(x)$$
Equivalently, if we write $$y = h(x) = g(u)$$ , where $$u = f(x)$$ , then
$$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{du}} \cdot \frac{\mathit{du}}{\mathit{dx}}$$

Equation (2) can be remembered by observing that if we “cancel” the $$\mathit{du}$$ ’s, then $$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{du}} \cdot \frac{\mathit{du}}{\mathit{dx}} = \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}}$$

section.heading: The Chain Rule for Powers of Functions
section.paragraph: Many composite functions have the special form $$h(x) = g\left( {f(x)} \right)$$ where $$g$$ is defined by the rule $$g(x) = x^{n}$$ ( $$n$$ , a real number)—that is,
$$h(x) = \left\lbrack f(x) \right\rbrack^{n}$$
In other words, the function $$h$$ is given by the power of a function $$f$$ . The functions

discussed earlier are examples of this type of composite function. By using the following corollary of the Chain Rule, the General Power Rule, we can find the derivative of this type of function much more easily than by using the Chain Rule directly.

note.title: The General Power Rule
note.heading: The General Power Rule
note.paragraph: If the function $$f$$ is differentiable and $$h(x) = \left\lbrack f(x) \right\rbrack^{n}$$ ( $$n$$ , a real number), then
$$h^{\prime}(x) = \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left\lbrack f(x) \right\rbrack^{n} = n\left\lbrack f(x) \right\rbrack^{n - 1}f^{\prime}(x)$$

section.paragraph: To see this, we observe that $$h(x) = g\left( f(x) \right)$$ where $$g(x) = x^{n}$$ , so by virtue of the Chain Rule, we have
$$\begin{array}{l} {h^{\prime}(x) = g^{\prime}\left\lbrack f(x) \right\rbrack f^{\prime}(x)} \\ {\phantom{h^{\prime}(x)} = n\left\lbrack f(x) \right\rbrack^{n - 1}f^{\prime}(x)} \end{array}$$
since $$g^{\prime}(x) = \mathit{nx}^{n - 1}$$ .

list.item: Find $$F^{\prime}(x)$$ , using the General Power Rule.
Verify your result without the benefit of the Chain Rule or the General Power Rule.

Using the General Power Rule, we obtain $$\begin{array}{l} {F^{\prime}(x) = 2{(3x + 1)}^{1}\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}(3x + 1)} \\ {\phantom{F^{\prime}(x)} = 2(3x + 1)(3)} \\ {\phantom{F^{\prime}(x)} = 6(3x + 1)} \end{array}$$

We first expand $$F(x)$$ . Thus, $$F(x) = (3x + 1)^{2} = 9x^{2} + 6x + 1$$ Next, differentiating, we have $$\begin{array}{l} {F^{\prime}(x) = \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}{({9x^{2} + 6x + 1})}} \\ {\phantom{F^{\prime}(x)} = 18x + 6} \\ {\phantom{F^{\prime}(x)} = 6\left( {3x + 1} \right)} \end{array}$$ as before.

note.source_type: Applied Example 7. Growth in a Health Club’s Membership
note.title: Applied Example 7. Growth in a Health Club’s Membership
note.heading: Applied Example 7. Growth in a Health Club’s Membership
note.paragraph: The membership of The Fitness Center, which opened a few years ago, is approximated by the function
where $$N(t)$$ gives the number of members at the beginning of week $$t$$ .

list.item: Find $$N^{\prime}(t)$$ .
How fast was the center’s membership increasing initially $$(t = 0)$$ ? (See Note.)
How fast was the membership increasing at the beginning of the $$40$$ th week?
What was the membership when the center first opened? At the beginning of the $$40$$ th week?

note.heading: Solution

list.item: Using the General Power Rule, we obtain $$\begin{array}{l} {N^{\prime}(t) = \frac{d}{\mathit{dt}}\left\lbrack 100{(64 + 4t)}^{2 \slash 3} \right\rbrack} \\ {\phantom{N^{\prime}(t)} = 100\frac{d}{\mathit{dt}}{(64 + 4t)}^{2 \slash 3}} \\ {\phantom{N^{\prime}(t)} = 100\left( \frac{2}{3} \right){(64 + 4t)}^{- 1 \slash 3}\frac{d}{\mathit{dt}}(64 + 4t)} \\ {\phantom{N^{\prime}(t)} = \frac{200}{3}{(64 + 4t)}^{- 1 \slash 3}(4)} \\ {\phantom{N^{\prime}(t)} = \frac{800}{3{(64 + 4t)}^{1 \slash 3}}} \end{array}$$
The rate at which the membership was increasing when the center first opened is given by $$N^{\prime}(0) = \frac{800}{3(64)^{1 \slash 3}} \approx 66.7$$ or approximately $$67$$ people per week.

The rate at which the membership was increasing at the beginning of the $$40$$ th week is given by $$N^{\prime}(40) = \frac{800}{3(64 + 160)^{1 \slash 3}} \approx 43.9$$ or approximately $$44$$ people per week.

The membership when the center first opened is given by $$N(0) = 100(64)^{2 \slash 3} = 100(16)$$ or approximately $$1600$$ people. The membership at the beginning of the $$40$$ th week is given by $$N(40) = 100(64 + 160)^{2 \slash 3} \approx 3688.3$$ or approximately $$3688$$ people.
